TCP congestion control has evolved substantially since Van Jacobson's original 1988 paper, which established the theoretical basis for both slow start and congestion avoidance, arguing from first principles that a sender must probe available capacity rather than assume it. Jacobson's insight was that the network itself gives no explicit signal about its carrying capacity, so the only reliable way to discover it is to increase the sending rate until loss occurs, then back off.

Slow start begins a connection at a small congestion window, typically one or a few maximum segment sizes, and doubles the window every round-trip time until either loss occurs or a threshold called ssthresh is reached. This exponential growth is deliberately aggressive at low rates, where the risk of causing serious congestion is small, and becomes more conservative as the window grows.

Once ssthresh is reached, or after a loss event resets it, the connection enters congestion avoidance, where the window grows linearly rather than exponentially — typically by one segment per round-trip time. This is the additive increase half of AIMD, additive increase multiplicative decrease, the name given to Jacobson's overall control law.

TCP Reno, an early and highly influential implementation, added fast retransmit to this picture. Fast retransmit triggers retransmission upon receipt of three duplicate ACKs, avoiding the costly wait for a retransmission timeout, which can be an order of magnitude slower to trigger. This alone was a significant improvement in recovery latency for isolated packet losses.

Reno's congestion window recovery after fast retransmit, however, halving cwnd and re-entering congestion avoidance, proved suboptimal for connections experiencing multiple losses within a single window. Because Reno could only reliably detect and recover from one loss per round-trip, a burst of losses would repeatedly halve the window, sometimes catastrophically, even when the underlying congestion event was a single, brief one.

This limitation motivated the development of Reno's successor, NewReno, which tracks partial ACKs during recovery to retransmit multiple lost segments without waiting for further timeouts or re-triggering the full fast-retransmit sequence for each one. NewReno's key mechanical change was distinguishing a "partial ACK," one that acknowledges some but not all of the outstanding data, from a full ACK that clears the recovery state entirely.

Separately from loss-based algorithms entirely, Google's BBR takes a fundamentally different approach to congestion control. Rather than treating packet loss as the primary congestion signal, BBR continuously models the network's bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation time, and paces its sending rate to match its own estimate of the bottleneck's capacity.

BBR's probing behavior periodically increases the pacing rate above its current estimate to re-discover whether more bandwidth has become available since the last measurement, a deliberate, bounded overshoot rather than the sustained additive growth AIMD-based algorithms use. This design choice means BBR does not depend on loss occurring at all to make forward progress, which is particularly relevant on links where loss can occur for reasons entirely unrelated to congestion, such as wireless interference.

The interaction between loss-based and model-based congestion control algorithms sharing the same bottleneck link remains an active and somewhat contested area of research. Because BBR does not back off in response to loss the way AIMD-based algorithms do, some studies have found that BBR flows can claim a disproportionate share of bandwidth when competing directly against Reno or CUBIC flows on a shared link, prompting ongoing revisions to BBR's fairness behavior in later versions.
